# One-Day Deep Dive Analysis: Day X (2026-07-19)

*Read-only extraction and analysis. Generated by `scripts/day_coverage.py`,
`scripts/extract_day.py`, `scripts/snap_gps.py` and
`scripts/extract_day_context.py`. No application code was modified.*

## Why Day X is 2026-07-19 and not the busiest day

The brief proposed the busiest day in 2026-01-01..2026-06-30 by truck count.
**That window contains no haul-truck GPS at all**, so it could not have proven
the join. Measured, on 2026-06-26 (the busiest day, 2,005 trips) exactly **0 of
the 121 plates** in `FMS_PLAYBACK_TRACK_DATA` are weighbridge haul trucks — that
table is 219 `SS###`/`E###` support units.

Searching every date for trucks with **both** a weighbridge trip and GPS on the
same day gives four candidates, all inside the raw-GPS retention window:

| Date | Trucks with both | Trips | GPS fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2026-07-19** | **24** | **26** | **11,584** |
| 2026-07-16 | 15 | 19 | 3,580 |
| 2026-07-15 | 14 | 21 | 3,581 |
| 2026-07-18 | 1 | 1 | 172 |

Day X is therefore **2026-07-19**, the widest overlap that exists. It is a small
sample, and that is stated wherever it matters.

Trips come from `HAULAGE`, not `HAULAGE_IWIP_CLEAN`: the CLEAN view stops at
2026-07-09, before any haul-truck GPS. `HAULAGE` runs to 2026-07-28 and shares
the same truck vocabulary (644 of 645 GPS haul trucks appear in it).

## Data pipeline proof

### GPS-to-weighbridge crosswalk

The two databases use three identifier namespaces, and confusing them is what
produced the earlier false "0 of 940" conclusion.

| Key | Format | Joins to |
|---|---|---|
| `HAULAGE.TRUCK_ID` | `B035`, `R280` | the weighbridge |
| `FMS_EQUIPMENTS.plateNumber` | `K977`, `A843` | **945 of 1,411 match the weighbridge** |
| `FMS_EQUIPMENTS.truckId` | `6916297240046994306` | the GPS tables only |
| `FMS_GPS_Historical.PLATE` | `B280` | **the weighbridge directly** |

**No crosswalk is actually needed.** `FMS_GPS_Historical` and
`FMS_PLAYBACK_TRACK_24H` carry a `PLATE` column in fleet-number format, so GPS
joins to the weighbridge without going through `FMS_EQUIPMENTS`. The 19-digit
`truckId` is a telematics device serial and matches **0** weighbridge trucks,
which is what the earlier work mistook for absence of instrumentation.

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Trucks in the crosswalk | 1,411 |
| Trucks in the weighbridge on Day X | 101 |
| Matched (GPS present) | **24 (23.8%)** |
| Unmatched | 77 — no GPS fix on Day X; the raw feed covered only **06:34–12:28 UTC**, roughly half the day |

### Segment-level speeds (from GPS)

Snapping method: **nearest `HAUL_ROAD_STA` chainage marker by great-circle
distance**. Markers sit every 25 m, so chainage error is bounded at ~12.5 m,
far below the 1 km reporting segments. Interpolation along the polyline would
add complexity without accuracy at this resolution. Fixes further than 150 m
from any marker are labelled **off-road** rather than snapped, because forcing
them onto a road would invent travel that never happened.

- **82.0%** of the 11,584 fixes snapped within 150 m
- **median snap distance 12.0 m**
- roads covered: **TOFU** (KM 39.0–67.8, 5,594 fixes) and **KR** (KM 15.9–39.0, 3,908 fixes)

| Section | Loaded (km/h) | Empty (km/h) | Obs | Trucks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KR KM32-33 | 21.3 | — | 2 | 2 |
| KR KM33-34 | 29.0 | — | 2 | 2 |
| KR KM34-35 | 16.6 | — | 2 | 2 |
| KR KM16-17 | 20.7 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM17-18 | 28.0 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM18-19 | 12.2 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM19-20 | 24.0 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM20-21 | 23.9 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM21-22 | 20.6 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM28-29 | — | 11.7 | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM30-31 | 30.1 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM31-32 | 24.6 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM35-36 | 15.3 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM36-37 | 17.2 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM37-38 | 5.1 | — | 1 | 1 |
| KR KM38-39 | 2.5 | — | 1 | 1 |

**The mechanism works. The sample does not support publishing these numbers.**
Most segments have n=1. Direction is signed from whether chainage rises or falls,
which separates loaded from empty legs, but only one empty observation survived.

Two independent checks say the *method* is sound even though the *sample* is thin:

1. **Median GPS-derived speed is 20.6 km/h.** `FMS_CONGESTION_SEG`, computed by
   the FMS itself from the same feed, reports a median of **17.2 km/h**. Two
   independent pipelines landing 3 km/h apart is a genuine cross-check.
2. **A clock-offset sensitivity test** (below) moves the median only between
   **20.6 and 25.4 km/h**.

### An unresolved clock ambiguity, and why it does not change the conclusion

`HAULAGE` stores clock times (`TIME_LOADED`, `TIME_EMPTY`), not datetimes, so
trip windows had to be reconstructed. Shifting those windows by −8 h more than
triples the number of matched fixes (402 → 1,360), which raises the question of
whether the ticket clock is local time while GPS is UTC.

**I did not adopt the shift that maximises matches.** With 24 trucks moving all
day, some offset will always look better, and optimising for it is how a false
result gets manufactured. Evidence gathered instead:

- `TS` and `RECEIVE_TIME` on the same GPS row agree to **3 seconds**, so GPS
  epochs are internally consistent.
- The two ticket clocks (`HAULAGE.TIME_LOADED` and
  `HAULAGE_IWIP_CLEAN.FIRST_WB_TIME`) correlate at **r = 0.904** across the
  hour-of-day profile, so they share one convention.
- Correlating the geofence hour profile against the ticket profiles gave **no
  clean peak** (best r = 0.406 at an implausible +4 h), so it is inconclusive.

So the offset stays at **0** and the ambiguity is reported. Its consequence is
bounded:

| Assumed offset | Trips matched | Segments | Median km/h |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 (used)** | 6 | 16 | **20.6** |
| −7 h | 8 | 21 | 23.1 |
| −8 h | 7 | 13 | 21.8 |
| −9 h | 9 | 13 | 22.3 |
| +7 h | 2 | 21 | 25.3 |
| +8/+9 h | 1 | 15 | 25.4 |

**The speed estimate is stable (20.6–25.4 km/h) regardless of offset; only the
sample size moves.** The pipeline conclusion holds either way. Resolving the
offset with the site would increase n, not change the answer.

### Dwell times (from GPS)

Method: the longest contiguous run under 2 km/h before the trip midpoint is
taken as loading, the longest after it as dumping. This is an inference from
movement, not a geofence event.

| Source | Trips | Median load (min) | Median dump (min) | Median cycle (min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TOS_TF_08 | 4 | 0.2 | 0.8 | 125.5 |
| TOS_TF_SMA_04 | 2 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 684.0 |

**This did not work, and the reason is instructive.** Near-zero dwell is not
credible for a 125-minute cycle. The GPS window covers only 06:34–12:28 UTC,
so for most trips the fixes captured are mid-haul and the actual loading and
tipping events fall outside the retained window. **GPS-derived dwell needs
full-day GPS retention.**

`WAITING_TIME` measures the same quantity directly and does join: **47 of 101
Day X trucks (46.5%)**, giving a measured **7.0 min load** and **2.0 min dump**.
That is the source to use for dwell, not GPS.

### Loader assignment

`EQUIPMENTS_HOURLY_ACTIVITIES` has 3,130 rows for Day X with 124 trucks and 10
excavators — and **0 of 101** Day X trucks match.

**The cause is not a namespace split.** I had previously reported an
`ADT4059`-vs-`A342` "namespace split"; that was wrong. `EQUIPMENTS.TYPE` shows
**`ADT` is a vehicle type — Articulated Dump Truck, contractor PPP, 40 t** — and
`EQUIPMENTS.ID_EQ` contains both vocabularies (all 124 ADT codes and 59 of the
101 Day X fleet numbers). So Day X simply had **a different fleet mining**: PPP's
articulated trucks were feeding the excavators while RIM's 30 t rigid dump trucks
(`TYPE = DT`, all 59 classified) were hauling.

Checked further, because "blocked" would have been the wrong conclusion:

- **746 of 1,382** `HOURLY_ACTIVITIES` trucks exist in `HAULAGE`, so the join
  works in general.
- Only **26 of 1,382** exist in `HAULAGE_IWIP_CLEAN`, the extract the models are
  trained on, and those have an excavator assigned on just **23 days**, peaking
  at 8 trucks (2026-04-21).

So loader assignment is **joinable but sparse**: it is not a format problem, it
is a coverage problem, and it will not support a fleet-wide loader feature.

`FMS_TRUCK_ASSIGNMENTS` has 70 Day X rows in weighbridge truck format, which is
the more promising source going forward despite its small size.

### Operator identity

| Source | Day X rows | Joins to Day X trucks |
|---|---|---|
| `DAY_WORKS` | 121 | **0** — `UNIT_ID` uses asset codes (`AR055`, `VRVV11011`), and `OPERATOR_ID` was empty for Day X |
| `WAITING_TIME` | 2,306 | **47 of 101 trucks (46.5%)**, with **958 distinct `DRIVER_ID`** |

`WAITING_TIME.DRIVER_ID` is the usable route to operator identity: numeric IDs,
per haul, joinable on truck. `DAY_WORKS` covers graders and support equipment by
asset code, not haul trucks by fleet number, so it is the wrong table for this.

Operator *experience* is derivable in principle by counting hauls per
`DRIVER_ID` over history, but that was not attempted here.

### Availability — measured, but NOT the win I first reported

> **Correction after scaling out.** This section originally called availability
> the highest-value immediate change. Checking whether it generalises beyond Day
> X shows it does not: across **215 days**, hauling-truck availability averages
> **83.6%** against the assumed 85% — a **1.4 pp** difference worth under 2% on
> tonnage. Day X's 89.4% was on the high side, not representative.
>
> The check was still worth running, because it uncovered a far more serious
> defect in how the simulator turns cycle time into trips. See
> **[CRITICAL_cycle_time_defect.md](CRITICAL_cycle_time_defect.md)**: the
> simulator divides by the weigh-to-weigh interval (median 76.9 min) when the
> true start-to-start cycle is **240.1 min**, so it **overpredicts production by
> ~2.7x**. That is the finding that matters, and it needs no GPS to fix.

#### The Day X measurement

`EQUIPMENTS_HOURLY_STATUS`, 17,692 rows for Day X across 2,733 units, 49 of them
Day X haul trucks.

| Measure | Fleet-wide | Trucks that hauled Day X |
|---|---|---|
| Availability, 1 − (BD+PM)/total | **76.5%** | **89.4%** |
| Utilisation, working / available | 45.1% | 69.7% |

Hours: working 23,092.4, standby 28,055.8, breakdown 15,400.2, PM 291.6.

#### Scaled across 215 days

| Population | Mean availability | Mean utilisation |
|---|---|---|
| All equipment | **77.0%** | 57.2% |
| Trucks that hauled (192 days, ~278/day) | **83.6%** | 78.0% |
| Simulator assumption | 85% | — |

Day X's availability of 76.5% fleet-wide sits at the **45th percentile**, so the
day itself is typical; it was the *hauling subset* figure of 89.4% that was high.
Only **2 of 215 days** fall within 2 pp of 85% fleet-wide, but the hauling subset
averages 83.6%, which is what the simulator actually models.

**Conclusion: the 85% assumption is close enough that replacing it changes
tonnage by under 2%.** Fleet-wide utilisation of 57.2% remains an interesting
operational number — over 40% of available equipment-hours are standby — but it
is not the simulator's bug.

### HRM fleet

`FMS_HRM_SUPERVISION`, 4,415 rows for Day X, **134 units**, 3,718 with GPS
coordinates, section KM 0–70 across BLB, CBB, CBBB, CRD, CSW, KR, TF, WD.

| Type | Rows |
|---|---|
| GD (grader) | 1,704 |
| EX (excavator) | 1,229 |
| CP (compactor) | 1,032 |
| WT (water truck) | 376 |
| DT | 34 |

Units per KM section (top): KR KM11 = 17 units, CBB KM14 = 11, KR KM18 = 10,
KR KM15 = 10, CBB KM15 = 10, TF KM51 = 10.

**This works well.** HRM presence is countable per KM section per day, which is
exactly the form needed to test whether road maintenance affects haul speed on
the same segments.

## What worked

1. **GPS-to-weighbridge identity.** `PLATE` joins directly, no crosswalk needed. 24 of 101 trucks on Day X, and the mechanism is exact, not fuzzy.
2. **Snapping GPS to KM chainage.** 82% of fixes within 150 m, median error 12 m, using 3,122 markers across 8 roads.
3. **Segment speeds with direction.** 19 observations over 16 segments, loaded and empty separated by chainage sign, cross-validated against `FMS_CONGESTION_SEG` (20.6 vs 17.2 km/h).
4. **Trip-to-GPS windowing.** No fuzzy matching required: exact truck identity plus a measured weigh-to-weigh interval.
5. **Availability from `EQUIPMENTS_HOURLY_STATUS`.** Real numbers replacing an assumption.
6. **HRM per KM section.** 134 units mapped to chainage with GPS.
7. **Measured dwell from `WAITING_TIME`.** 46.5% of Day X trucks, 7.0 min load, 2.0 min dump.
8. **Offset sensitivity bounded.** The unresolved clock question changes n, not the speed conclusion.

## What did not work

1. **GPS-derived dwell.** Near-zero values are not credible; the GPS window covers only 06:34–12:28 UTC, so loading and tipping events mostly fall outside it. Needs full-day retention. Use `WAITING_TIME` instead.
2. **Loader assignment on Day X.** `EQUIPMENTS_HOURLY_ACTIVITIES` was recording a different fleet (PPP articulated trucks) while RIM rigid trucks hauled. Joinable in general (746 of 1,382 trucks) but only 26 overlap the training extract, across 23 days.
3. **`DAY_WORKS` for operators.** Asset codes, not fleet numbers, and `OPERATOR_ID` empty for Day X. Wrong table for haul trucks.
4. **77 of 101 trucks have no GPS.** Partial-day retention, not missing instrumentation.
5. **The clock offset is unresolved.** Three probes were inconclusive. Bounded, documented, not guessed.

## Conclusion

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Can we build segment-level speeds from GPS? | **Yes, mechanically proven.** 19 observations over 16 segments, direction-aware, cross-validated. Needs more retention for statistical weight. |
| Can we model queue at loading/dumping from GPS? | **Not from the current GPS window.** Partial-day retention misses the terminal events. **Yes from `WAITING_TIME`**, which measures it directly at 46.5% coverage. |
| Can we get loader assignment? | **Partially.** Format is fine; coverage is not. 26 trucks over 23 days against the training extract. `FMS_TRUCK_ASSIGNMENTS` is the better forward source. |
| Can we get operator identity? | **Yes**, via `WAITING_TIME.DRIVER_ID` (958 drivers, 46.5% of trucks). Not via `DAY_WORKS`. |
| Can we replace assumed availability with real data? | **Yes, but it barely matters.** 83.6% for hauling trucks over 215 days vs the assumed 85% — under 2% on tonnage. |
| Can we test HRM impact? | **Yes.** 134 units per day mapped to KM sections with GPS. |

### What this means for scaling

The pipeline is proven end to end: identity, snapping, trip windowing, segment
speeds and direction all work on real data. **The binding constraint is GPS
retention, not the method.** Day X yielded 24 trucks and 6 usable trips because
the raw feed keeps days, not months, and covered only half of Day X itself.

Two consequences:

1. **Scaling backwards is not possible** for segment speeds. The historical
   trips the models were trained on have no GPS, and no amount of processing
   creates it.
2. **Scaling forwards is straightforward.** `scripts/extract_day.py --day` and
   `scripts/snap_gps.py` re-run for any date. Accumulating the live feed daily
   from now would build the segment-speed history that does not yet exist. At
   Day X density (~440 trucks per day in `FMS_GEOFENCE_VISITS`), a month of
   capture would give a usable sample.

The immediately actionable finding needs no GPS at all, and it is not the one I
first reported. Verifying whether the availability result generalised revealed
that **the simulator overpredicts production by ~2.7x**, because it divides the
shift by the weigh-to-weigh interval (76.9 min) rather than the true
start-to-start cycle (240.1 min), measured over 438,992 consecutive trip pairs.
`720 / 240.1 = 3.00` trips, exactly the observed median.

Full evidence and a proposed fix: **[CRITICAL_cycle_time_defect.md](CRITICAL_cycle_time_defect.md)**.
The ratio varies by route from 1.2x to 7.9x, so it needs a per-route measured
cycle rather than a global constant. It requires no GPS and covers the whole
history.
